answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Azure resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for a cluster/account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (child resources like MongoDB databases/collections are under that account).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create: az cosmosdb create --name my-docdb-account --resource-group my-rg --locations regionName=westus --default-consistency-level Strong --kind MongoDB. (az cosmosdb is part of the core az CLI, not a separate extension.)

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer:
Bicep/ARM: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Example Bicep resource declaration: resource docdb 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myDocDb' location: resourceGroup().location properties: { locations: [ { locationName: resourceGroup().location } ] kind: 'MongoDB' capabilities: [ { name: 'EnableMongo' } ] } }
Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account. Example: resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "docdb" { name = "my-docdb" location = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" ... }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical MongoDB-compatible connection string: either mongodb:// or mongodb+srv://. Hostname pattern: <account-name>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com (or <account>.documents.azure.com for some accounts); common port is 10255 for TLS. Example: mongodb://myUser:myPassword@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. If using SRV: mongodb+srv://myUser:myPassword@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Required options usually include ssl=true (TLS) and replicaSet=globaldb and often retryWrites=false for Cosmos-style Mongo endpoints.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is typically provisioned as a managed cluster tier (named tiers like M10/M30 etc. in this environment) priced by compute (vCores/instance class) plus storage; it is not the Cosmos DB RU model for this MongoDB-compatible offering. There may also be serverless or autoscale flavors in some SKUs, but for this sample you should use the M30 compute tier as provided.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary supported data-plane auth methods: standard MongoDB username/password (SCRAM-SHA-1 or SCRAM-SHA-256) and TLS/X.509 client certificate auth when enabled. Some managed offerings also support Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) token-based auth, but that typically requires obtaining an Azure AD access token and supplying it to the driver (using the driver SASL/OAUTHBEARER or passing the token as the password depending on driver support). In practice for immediate coding use, use the provided username/password credential in the connection string (SCRAM) or a client X.509 cert. If using Azure AD, obtain an access token for the service principal and pass it to the driver per the provider documentation (this flow is provider-specific).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For data-plane access use standard MongoDB drivers (for Python: pymongo or motor). There is no special proprietary data-plane SDK required for MongoDB-compatible DocumentDB clusters; for management you can use azure-cli/azure-sdk management libraries (azure-mgmt-cosmosdb or azure-native in IaC).

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Supported vector index methods in MongoDB-7-style syntax: HNSW, IVF, DiskANN (depending on cluster build). Create example (Mongo shell / pymongo): db.positions.createIndex( { embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'embedding_knn', 'knnVector': { 'dimensions': 1536, 'method': 'hnsw', 'similarity': 'cosine', 'efConstruction': 200, 'M': 16 } } ). For DiskANN or IVF replace method:'diskann' or method:'ivf' and supply method-specific params.

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Simple full‑text: use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' })) for basic text search. For advanced hybrid vector+text retrieval use the engine's integrated search if available (a $search/$searchMeta aggregation stage in Atlas-style deployments) or combine vector similarity queries with text scoring in application logic. On Azure you can also integrate with Azure Cognitive Search for richer hybrid search scenarios if the managed Mongo-compatible engine does not provide a Lucene-style search stage.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: This cluster advertises MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol compatibility. Commonly restricted or different features on managed Mongo-compatible services include: server-side JavaScript ($where), some admin/diagnostic commands, custom storage-engine options, and in certain SKUs multi-document transactions or certain change-stream/topology features can be limited. Expect standard CRUD, aggregation pipeline, and new vector index features to work, but verify unsupported commands in the service docs or by testing.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no perfect official Azure-native local emulator for the MongoDB-compatible cluster. For local development run the official MongoDB docker image (e.g. mongo:7.0) and bind to port 27017: docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo mongo:7.0. Use that for running aggregation and vector logic locally if the server supports the same features; otherwise test against the live cluster.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams (watch()) are supported on replica-set style MongoDB clusters; on managed MongoDB-compatible offerings they are often available but may require an appropriate SKU/tier and that the deployment maintain an oplog. No extra client-side enablement is normally required beyond using a driver that supports watch() and connecting with a user that has read privileges. Verify by running db.collection.watch() in your environment.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb-specific MCP server (documentdb) to get MongoDB-aware data-plane tooling and inspection (the environment statement references a 'documentdb' MCP server). The generic Azure MCP server may not include MongoDB-specific helpers (index/model inspectors, explain plan viewers) so prefer the documentdb MCP server for data-plane operations.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft had an internal DocumentDB offering that evolved into Azure Cosmos DB; 'DocumentDB' is an older Microsoft name and is distinct from the open-source 'DocumentDB' projects elsewhere. The current managed MongoDB-compatible service is a separate managed offering (exposed via Microsoft.DocumentDB provider for ARM) that provides a MongoDB wire-compatible endpoint; it is not the same as the old DocumentDB SQL API but is related in the Azure ecosystem.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is a MongoDB‑compatible engine (either a MongoDB-compatible server implementation provided by the service or a MongoDB distribution). From an application perspective you should use standard MongoDB drivers and the MongoDB wire protocol; most CRUD/aggregation code is unchanged. However some server-side features, admin commands, and edge-case behaviors may differ, so test features like transactions, server-side JS, and certain aggregation stages against the target cluster.

answers.question: What database name should the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_banking_17 for everything the sample creates and reads.

answers.question: What collection and index definitions will the sample create for positions and embeddings?
answers.answer: Create a positions collection and indexes: 1) standard compound index on accountId and instrumentId for fast lookups: db.positions.createIndex({ accountId: 1, instrumentId: 1 }) 2) vector knn index on embedding field (example 1536-dim, HNSW): db.positions.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'embedding_knn', knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', efConstruction: 200, M: 16 } })

answers.question: What aggregation pipeline will the impact agent run to compute P&L under a shock?
answers.answer:
Example pipeline (pseudocode using MongoDB aggregation stages):
[ { $match: { accountId: <account>, instrumentId: { $in: <instruments> } } }, { $project: { accountId:1, instrumentId:1, quantity:1, price:1, shockedPrice: { $multiply: ["$price", { $add: [1, "$scenario.shockPct"] } ] } } }, { $project: { pnl: { $multiply: ["$quantity", { $subtract: ["$shockedPrice", "$price"] } ] }, instrumentId:1, accountId:1 } }, { $group: { _id: "$accountId", totalPnl: { $sum: "$pnl" }, perInstrument: { $push: { instrumentId: "$instrumentId", pnl: "$pnl" } } } } ]
Run with db.positions.aggregate(pipeline) and pass scenario.shockPct as parameter in the pipeline or substitute before running.

answers.question: What schema will the sample use to store scenario runs for audit?
answers.answer:
Scenario run document example: { _id: ObjectId(), runId: 'run-20261125-001', createdAt: ISODate(), scenario: { shockPct: 0.10, shockType: 'price_drop', generatedBy: 'scenario-agent', params: {...} }, results: { totalPnl: 12345.67, perAccount: [...], perInstrument: [...] }, metadata: { durationMs: 1234, aggregationPipelineHash: 'sha256...', indexesChecked: ['embedding_knn'] }, status: 'completed' }
Store these in a collection named scenario_runs (db.scenario_runs.insertOne(...)).

answers.question: Exactly how will the sample authenticate to the cluster in code using the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI?
answers.answer:
Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it straight to pymongo.MongoClient. Example (Python):
from os import environ
from pymongo import MongoClient
uri = environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']
# Example URI already contains username/password and options (ssl=true,...)
client = MongoClient(uri)
db = client['sample_banking_17']
# Do not print or write the URI anywhere; use secure runtime environment variables.
If the URI is SRV form (mongodb+srv://) the driver will resolve the SRV record automatically. Ensure TLS is enabled in the URI (ssl=true) and the driver is configured for TLS verification in production.
